how-much-to-charge-to-build-a-wheelchair.text:
Wheelchair ramp bid calculator

How much to charge to build a wheelchair ramp

A published “$85 a lineal foot” special prices the sloped run. A residential wheelchair ramp is not a run. It is a rise, a slope, a pair of landings at the door and at grade, a rest landing once the rise crosses about 30 inches, a turn landing on a switchback, both-side handrails, and footings. Matching the coupon on a 36-inch wood switchback is how a sold job becomes a two-day loss after the first rest landing.

Open the free bid calculator

The number a lineal-foot special cannot see

Take a 24-inch rise at a 1:12 starting slope and a 4-foot width. The run is 24 lineal feet — 96 square feet of sloped walking surface. Two 5-by-5 landings add 50 square feet. That is 146 square feet of walking surface, and the landings are more than a third of it. The coupon still says “24 feet.”

Raise the same opening to 36 inches. The run becomes 36 lineal feet, and a rest landing typically appears. The walking surface is no longer “36 feet of ramp.” It is the sloped run plus three landings. A switchback on a 24-inch rise adds a turn landing the straight coupon never priced at all.

How to price it

  1. Measure the rise in inches, from finished grade to the threshold.
  2. Convert to run: rise × run-per-rise ÷ 12. Twelve inches of run per inch of rise is the common 1:12 starting point, not a determination that the layout is compliant.
  3. Count landings: top, bottom, a rest landing whenever the rise exceeds the interval you are using, and a turn landing when a switchback did not already rest.
  4. Add both-side handrails when the rise is above your threshold, footings along the run, stair demo if you are pulling the existing steps, and the permit allowance.
  5. Load the wage, add materials and mobilization, mark overhead on direct cost, then divide by one minus the target margin. The walk-away price is total cost.

The wheelchair ramp bid calculator does that arithmetic in the browser from your own hours and invoices. Starting slope ratios, landing sizes, and material rates are ballpark figures to replace, not a catalog or a code table.

What this is not

This is not an ADA determination, a building-code opinion, a permit, a construction specification, or an engineering stamp. Confirm the jurisdiction, the occupant, and a qualified professional before sending a price. The output is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

No warranty. This free article and calculator are not construction, legal, tax, financial, or engineering advice. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from their use.

Common questions

How much to charge to build a wheelchair ramp?

Start from the rise, convert it to run at the slope you are actually building, then add every landing, both-side handrail, footing, demo, and permit. A published $85 per lineal foot special only sees the sloped run.

Why do landings change the price?

A 24-inch rise at 1:12 is 24 lineal feet of run. Two 5-by-5 landings add 50 square feet that never appear in that lineal-foot number. A 36-inch rise typically adds a rest landing as well.

Is this an ADA or code calculation?

No. Slope ratios and landing sizes here are common starting points on residential bids. They are not an ADA determination, a building-code opinion, a permit, or an engineering stamp.

FOR ACCESSIBILITY AND DECK CREWS

Bid the landings, the rails, and the rise.

Price a residential wheelchair ramp built to an ADA-style 1:12 slope the way the trade actually loses money: rise to run, then every landing a lineal-foot special cannot see, both-side handrails, surface, demo, permit, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the job price, what it works out to per foot of run and per walking square foot, and the number below which the job loses money.

Looking up how much to charge to build a wheelchair ramp? Start here, then replace every starting figure with your own crew times.

A starting job

Pick a common call to fill the rise, slope, layout, and surface. Changing a kit never overwrites hours or material costs you have already typed.

The opening

Rise is the step from grade to the threshold. Slope is inches of run per inch of rise — 1:12 is twelve inches of run for each inch of rise. These are starting points, not a code opinion.

Hours and extras

Hours per 100 sf apply to the whole walking surface — sloped run plus every landing. Handrail and footing counts start from the geometry; change them when the site disagrees.

Materials and your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. A lineal-foot special written on the run never sees it — or the landings.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting slopes, landing sizes, hours, and material rates are common ballpark figures, not an ADA determination, a building-code opinion, a permit, a warranty, or an engineering stamp. Time your own crews and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why is a 24-inch rise ramp 146 sq ft of walking surface, not 24 feet of ramp?

    Because a lineal-foot special counts the sloped run and stops there. At a 1:12 slope, a 24-inch rise needs 24 lf of run, which at 4 ft wide is 96 sq ft — but the top and bottom landings add another 50 sq ft at the default 5×5 size, for 146 sq ft of actual walking surface. The lf number a competitor quotes off of never included the two landings the ramp can't function without.

    Why does a switchback sometimes need an extra landing that a straight ramp of the same rise doesn't?

    Because a switchback needs a turn platform, and if the rise is short enough that no rest landing is already required between the top and bottom landings, the turn itself still has to happen somewhere — so the calculator adds one landing specifically for that case. A straight run at that same short rise needs only its top and bottom landings; the switchback layout is what forces the extra one.

    Why does aluminum cost so much more per square foot than wood, and why does it have no framing cost?

    A modular aluminum kit prices decking at $28 per sq ft against $4.50 for pressure-treated wood, but it carries zero framing cost because the modular structure is the surface — there's no separate joist-and-post build the way wood, composite, and concrete all need at $4–$6 per sq ft. Aluminum also cuts labor roughly in half, at 1.8 hours per 100 sq ft versus 3.2 for wood, so the two costs move in opposite directions.

    Why does the calculator suggest zero handrail footage below a 6-inch rise?

    Because that's the common starting threshold below which handrails are often not required on a residential ramp — the suggestion is editable, and the shop can still add rail hours and footage for any rise. Above the threshold, suggested handrail length covers both sides of the run plus one side of every landing, which is why landing count feeds into rail footage as well as surface area.

    Why does the footing count grow with both the run length and the number of landings?

    Footings come from three sources added together: a fixed pair at the house, a pair at every landing, and posts spaced along the run itself — by default one pair roughly every 8 feet. A longer run needs more posts along its length independent of landings, and more landings need their own support independent of run length, so a switchback with an extra landing on a long run can need noticeably more footings than a straight ramp of the same total rise.

    Do this calculator's defaults match ADA ramp requirements?

    The defaults mirror the numbers most often cited from the ADA Standards for Accessible Design: a 1:12 maximum running slope, a landing at least every 30 inches of rise, 5×5 ft (60×60 in) landings, and handrails once rise passes 6 inches — which is exactly what this calculator starts from. Matching those numbers is not the same as certifying ADA compliance: the standard also covers surface texture, handrail height and grip diameter, edge protection, and cross slope, none of which this calculator checks. Verify the built ramp against the full standard, your local building code, or the authority having jurisdiction before calling a job compliant.

    Does a ramp at a private home have to meet ADA requirements?

    Not automatically. The ADA's design standards are a legal requirement for places of public accommodation and commercial facilities; a single-family home generally sits outside that reach unless it was built with certain public funds, falls under a state or local accessibility code, or the ramp is a condition of a program such as a VA or state home-modification grant. Plenty of homeowners ask for “ADA” anyway because it is the slope everyone recognizes, which is why the defaults above start there — confirm which rules actually apply to your job before pricing to a different slope.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-lineal-foot.html.text:
← Wheelchair Ramp Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per lineal foot

“$X a lineal foot, any ramp” is not a price for a ramp build — it is a price for one rise, one layout, and one surface, quietly applied to a rise twice as tall that needs a rest landing, a switchback turn, and both-side handrail the coupon never saw.

What a flat rate per lineal foot is

A flat rate per lineal foot is the fastest way to quote a ramp over the phone: multiply the run by a number and read it back. Homeowners like it because it is easy to compare against a competitor's quote, and it is the number a customer holding one will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for the simplest version of the job — a short, straight run at the minimum slope, needing only the two required landings and a basic wood surface — and then reused for every ramp afterward, whether or not the next one is tall enough to need a rest landing, turns a switchback, or goes on a pricier surface.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the rise, slope, layout (straight or switchback), surface, width, whether to demo existing stairs, and whether to include a permit, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It converts rise and slope to run, adds every landing the layout and rise require, prices the walking surface by material, prices both-side handrail and footings separately, and returns the price, the price per lineal foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price — for this ramp, not a flat rate for every ramp.

What a flat rate per lineal foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same per foot whether the rise needs only the two required landings or a rest landing and a switchback turn on top of them. Counts every landing the rise and layout require — intermediate rest landings at the maximum-rise interval, plus a turn landing for a switchback that did not already rest — and prices the walking surface from run plus every landing, not run alone.
Has no line for both-side handrail, even though handrail lineal footage grows with the run and every landing, not with the run alone. Prices handrail from the run and landing perimeter as its own line, separate from the walking surface.
Has no line for footings, which scale with both the run length and the landing count. Prices footings by count — a pair at the house, a pair per landing, and posts along the run — as its own line.
Charges the same rate for pressure-treated wood and for composite, aluminum, or poured concrete, even though the material cost per square foot can be several times higher. Prices the walking surface by the selected material's own decking and framing cost per square foot.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price, the profit, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two ramps, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own figures, at a 25% target margin, a $28 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, and $85 in travel and equipment:

A 24-inch rise, straight, pressure-treated wood ramp with the two required landings costs $4,601.99 to run and this calculator prices it at $6,135.98 — $255.67 per lineal foot. A 48-inch rise switchback on modular aluminum — a rest landing, a turn landing, 111 lf of handrail, 22 footings, a stair demo, and a permit — costs $13,910.58 to run and this calculator prices it at $18,547.43, 3.02 times the small ramp's price on just twice the run. Quote the aluminum switchback at the wood ramp's flat $255.67-per-foot rate instead, and 48 feet prices at $12,271.96 — $1,638.61 below the ramp's own break-even cost — before counting the $6,275.47 it falls short of what this calculator prices the ramp at. Same rate, one ramp that pays and one that loses money the moment the rest landing and the handrail show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per lineal foot get a taller ramp wrong?

Because lineal feet of run is not the walking surface, and it is not the parts list. A flat rate is usually set on a small straight run with the minimum two landings; a taller rise needs a rest landing the coupon never counted, a switchback needs a turn landing, and both-side handrail and footing counts grow with the landings, not with the run alone. Using this calculator's own figures, a 24-inch straight wood ramp costs $4,601.99 to run and prices at $6,135.98 -- $255.67 per lineal foot. A 48-inch switchback aluminum ramp with a rest landing, demo, and permit costs $13,910.58 to run and this calculator prices it at $18,547.43 -- 3.02 times the small ramp's price, not twice, on exactly twice the run.

What does a flat rate per lineal foot usually leave out entirely?

Landings, handrail, footings, and the surface material. A flat per-lf rate has no line for a rest landing a taller rise requires, no line for a switchback's turn landing, no line for both-side handrail lineal footage, no line for the footing count a longer run and more landings both add, and no line for a pricier surface like aluminum or concrete instead of wood. It also has no line for demoing existing stairs or pulling a permit.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own figures: the 24-inch straight wood ramp prices at $6,135.98, on a job that costs $4,601.99 to run, at $255.67 per lineal foot. Apply that same per-lf rate to the 48-inch switchback aluminum ramp (rest landing, demo, permit) and it quotes at $12,271.96 -- $1,638.61 below the ramp's own $13,910.58 break-even cost, before counting the $6,275.47 it falls short of what this calculator prices the ramp at ($18,547.43, 3.02 times the small ramp).

Is a flat rate per lineal foot ever the right way to quote?

For a ramp close to the rise, layout, and surface the rate was set on -- typically a short straight run needing only the two required landings -- a flat per-lf number can land close, because that is probably the ramp the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a rise tall enough to need a rest landing, a switchback, a pricier surface, a demo, or a permit at the same rate, because the rate does not know the rise, the layout, or the surface until someone measures the site, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's material pricing, or what other ramp builders in your area charge. It takes rise, slope, layout, surface, width, handrail, footings, demo, permit, and your own wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this ramp -- the arithmetic a flat rate per lineal foot skips, not a market survey or a code determination.

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a carpentry or accessibility-modification company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this wheelchair ramp cost, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — general contracting, handyman work, carpentry, and remodeling among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Public research puts its founding in 2011, headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, and reports it is used by more than 200,000 service professionals. Its own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home service field service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing, and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a wheelchair ramp should cost from its rise, landings, and rails before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes a residential wheelchair ramp — rise-to-run geometry, intermediate or switchback landings, both-side handrails, a wood, composite, aluminum, or concrete surface kit, demo of an existing structure, and a permit allowance — plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, where the bid's cost is actually coming from, a copyable customer-facing bid summary, and a printable customer proposal with scope lines, a deposit split, and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
